claims.text: At high temperatures, radiation-induced defect clusters mediate a transition from dislocation glide to dislocation climb in tungsten-based fusion plasma-facing materials.
The transition from dislocation glide to dislocation climb enhances plasticity.
The transition from dislocation glide to dislocation climb enhances toughness.
Controlled radiation exposure generates defect clusters in tungsten-based specimens.
Radiation-induced defect clusters impede dislocation glide.
Impeded dislocation glide necessitates dislocation climb at high temperatures.
Dislocation climb induced by radiation-created defect clusters increases strain-hardening capability.
Dislocation climb induced by radiation-created defect clusters increases toughness.
Radiation-induced defect clusters may increase yield strength.
Radiation-pre-exposed specimens will have higher high-temperature yield strength than unexposed controls.
Radiation-pre-exposed specimens will exhibit more pronounced high-temperature strain hardening than unexposed controls.
Radiation-pre-exposed specimens will contain a greater density of defect clusters than unexposed controls.
Greater defect-cluster density will correlate with modified dislocation patterns.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to tungsten and tungsten-based alloys at approximately 800–1200°C when thermal activation and radiation effects are significant.
A direct in situ correlation between radiation-induced defect clusters and a glide-to-climb transition under relevant fusion conditions has not been unequivocally demonstrated.
The proposed response may vary with tungsten-alloy composition.
The proposed response may vary with radiation dose.
Irradiated and pristine specimens are to be tested under identical temperatures and mechanical-loading conditions.
Failure to observe statistically significant increases in yield strength and strain hardening together with the expected microstructural changes would falsify the hypothesis.
